Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA comer Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City http: //www.dilg.com.ph DILG OPINION No. 26 s. 2023 APR poa HON. BENJAMIN B. MAGALONG Mayor, Baguio City Dear Mayor Magalong: This has reference to your letter dated December 12, 2022 requesting clarification on the applicable rules and guidelines that may be adopted in support of your proposed congestion fee charging scheme in the City of Baguio. It is understood that the proposed imposition of congestion fee by the City of Baguio is for the general welfare of its constituents and its visiting tourists which is in accordance with Section 16 of R.A. No. 7160, otherwise known as the "Local Government Code of 1991". We respectfully submit, therefore, that there is no legal impediment for the City of Baguio's proposed congestion fees provided that the proposed ordinance had complied the ordinary safeguards for its validity, to wit: (I)t must not only be within the corporate powers of the local government unit to enact and must be passed according to the procedure prescribed by law, it must also conform to the following substantive requirements: (1) must not contravene the Constitution or any statute; (2) must not be unfair or oppressive; (3) must not be partial or discriminatory; (4) must not prohibit but may regulate trade; (5) must be general and consistent with public policy; and (6) must not be unreasonable.l The imposition of congestion fees is in line with the exercise of police power through taxation. This is well enunciated in the case of Progressive Dev. Corp vs. Quezon City2, viz: The term "tax" frequently applies to all kinds of exactions of monies which become public funds. It is often loosely used to include levies for revenue as well as levies for regulatory purposes such that license fees are frequently called taxes although license fee is a legal concept distinguishable from tax: the former is imposed in the exercise of police power primarily for purposes of regulation, while the latter is imposed under the taxing power primarily for purposes of raising revenues. 9 Thus, if the generating of revenue is the primary purpose and regulation is merely incidental, the imposition is a tax; but if regulation is the primary 1 G.R. No. 118127; April 12, 2005. 2 G.R. No. 36081; April 24, 1989. "Matino, Mahusay at Maaasahan" Trunkline No.: 8870-34-54

purpose, the fact that incidentally revenue is also obtained does not make the imposition a tax. Lutz vs. Araneta3 likewise stated that taxation may be made the implement of the state's police power. Along this line, please be informed also that there is published legal research conducted by Wilfred Francis B. Martinez from De La Salle University, College of Law, entitled "The Philippine congestion tax law: A solution to traffic congestion and the economic, environmental, and health problems that follow it'4. Stated in its abstract of the study is a conclusion that upon reading the relevant Philippine laws such as the 1987 Constitution of the Republic of the Philippines, Republic Act 8794, and various jurisprudence decided by the Supreme Court, it is clear that there is no legal impediment in the adoption of a Congestion Pricing scheme in the country thus a legislation enabling Congestion Pricing to be enacted is highly recommended. This opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities and the courts. We hope to have assisted you accordingly. Thank you. Very truly yours, Authority of the Secretary: ICTOR R. LLAMAS n ersecretary for External, Legal and Legislative Affairs OUSELlAJVULLLS-LRALLD/kbm/clp DIR. ARACELI A. SAN JOSE Regional Director, DILG CAR Region Barangay Center, Upper Session Road Cor. North Drive, Baguio City
